planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers once soil has warmed slightly; as a true late maincrop it needs the full growing season to size up and develop its characteristic dry matter.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and hill as shoots emerge, since this rough-skinned Scottish maincrop needs a long season to fully develop its dense, floury flesh. Found near Arbroath on Scotland's east coast in 1906, Golden Wonder became one of Britain's most recognizable heirloom potatoes, prized for its exceptionally high dry matter content that makes it outstanding for baking, roasting, and frying but prone to disintegrating if overboiled. The variety's reputation for superb crisp (chip) quality was significant enough that a major British snack-food brand took its name directly from the potato. Choose Golden Wonder over a modern maincrop when a genuinely dry, floury texture with deep, old-fashioned potato flavor matters more than smooth skin or high yield.

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers once soil is workable; this second-early landrace is less vigorous than modern cultivars and benefits from generous spacing and a longer, gentler hilling-up.

directions: Plant seed tubers 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil; Shetland Black is an old landrace potato grown for generations in Scotland's Shetland Islands, producing modest, uneven yields of small, dark maroon-to-black-skinned tubers. Sliced open, the creamy white flesh reveals a distinctive deep purple ring just beneath the skin, a trait unique enough that the variety is grown today mainly as a specialty and conservation crop rather than for volume. Its low, inconsistent cropping means it is best suited to a dedicated heritage bed rather than the main kitchen-garden potato patch, but the striking appearance and dense, waxy texture reward the extra care. Boil or steam whole to show off the purple ring in cross-section.

planting.note: Plant certified seed tubers once soil has warmed; as a late maincrop bred for disease tolerance it rewards a full-length season over poorer or wetter ground.

directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and hill generously, since this old Scottish maincrop carries more disease tolerance than many of its contemporaries and performs reliably even on indifferent ground. Bred on the Isle of Arran by farmer-breeder Donald MacKelvie, it was released to commemorate the end of the First World War and is immediately recognizable by its unusual violet-purple skin wrapped around pure white, floury flesh. MacKelvie went on to breed more than twenty Arran-named varieties, but Victory remains the most distinctive for its coloring and its place as one of the earliest successes of his program. Grow it for a genuinely old-pedigree maincrop with striking skin color and solid resistance where a fussier modern hybrid would struggle.

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees while dormant; Songold has a low winter-chilling requirement, making it one of the more reliable Japanese plums for mild-winter, Mediterranean-type climates. Provide a compatible pollinator for best fruit set.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun with a cross-pollinating plum nearby, and thin fruit while still marble-sized to improve final size and color. Songold was bred at South Africa's Infruitec-Nietvoorbij research station from a Wickson x Golden King cross and released in 1970, taking its portmanteau name from its parent cultivars. It is a clingstone Japanese plum with red-purple skin over firm yellow flesh, valued across South Africa's Western Cape for its low chilling requirement and its ability to crop heavily and consistently even in a warm winter. Alongside Laetitia, it remains one of the two plum cultivars grown in the greatest volume in South African commercial orchards, and performs well wherever winters are too mild for traditional European plum varieties.
sources: Agricultural Research Council of South Africa (ARC Infruitec-Nietvoorbij)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or containerized trees while dormant in a sheltered, full-sun site; provide a compatible Japanese plum pollinator nearby, as Laetitia sets fruit most heavily with cross-pollination.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in well-drained soil and thin young fruit to prevent limb breakage on this consistently heavy-bearing cultivar. Laetitia originated as an open-pollinated seedling of the Golden King plum discovered in a South African orchard in the early 1970s and was formally released by Infruitec-Nietvoorbij in 1985 after years of trial evaluation around Stellenbosch and Franschhoek. It is a freestone Japanese plum with attractive red skin over sweet, firm, amber-yellow flesh, maturing in mid-to-late season after most early plum cultivars have finished. Together with Songold, it anchors much of South Africa's commercial and export plum production and is a sound choice wherever a dependable, well-flavored freestone plum is wanted in a low-chill climate.
sources: Agricultural Research Council of South Africa (ARC Infruitec-Nietvoorbij)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant; Oom Sarel has a low winter-chilling requirement and is self-fertile, so it bears reliably in mild-winter regions without a second tree. Prune annually to control its naturally vigorous, spreading habit.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter in full sun and prune firmly each year, since this old South African heirloom, also sold as Kakamas, grows into a large, vigorous, spreading tree if left unchecked. It bears heavy crops of large, round, golden-yellow clingstone peaches with firm, flavorful yellow flesh, ripening in early-to-mid summer in its home climate. Being self-pollinating and low-chill, it produces dependably in warm-winter regions where many standard peach cultivars fail to set fruit, and the firm clingstone flesh holds up well to canning, drying, and baking in addition to fresh eating. It remains a favorite in South African home orchards for exactly this combination of reliability, productivity, and multipurpose fruit.
sources: Agricultural Research Council of South Africa

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; Pig Aderyn is self-sterile and needs a compatible pollination-group partner nearby.

directions: Plant a compatible pollinator nearby and prune to an open framework, since this old Welsh apple is self-sterile but crops well once paired correctly. Pig Aderyn has grown for centuries near St Dogmaels Abbey in Pembrokeshire, where tradition holds it was first cultivated by monks for cider, and takes its Welsh name, meaning 'bird's beak,' from the pointed shape at the fruit's crown. The oblate, yellow-skinned fruit is streaked with bright red and is genuinely multi-purpose: picked early it makes a light, tangy cider, left to mature it is an excellent cooking apple, and fully ripe it becomes a sweet, juicy dessert apple. This willingness to serve three different purposes from one tree, combined with its documented surviving specimens, has made it a focus of recent Welsh heritage-orchard conservation work.
sources: Welsh Perry & Cider Society / Welsh Heritage Pomona

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun; this late-ripening variety needs a long autumn to finish on the tree.

directions: Leave fruit on the tree as late as possible in autumn, since this 19th-century Welsh heirloom only reaches full flavor after a long, slow finish and continues to improve further in storage. Surviving old trees recorded at Dinefwr in Carmarthenshire are more than seventy years old, and little else is documented about the variety's deeper origins beyond its long local presence there. The medium-to-large fruit has yellow skin with an orange flush and some dry russeting around the stem, ripening in November and keeping in store into February, by which point its sharper young flavor mellows into a rich, aromatic sweetness. It can be eaten fresh once mellowed, but is most valued in Wales as a bittersweet cider apple, pressed for a cider noted locally for its depth of character.
sources: Welsh Perry & Cider Society / Welsh Heritage Pomona
